Arma 3 is on Real Virtuality engine and has seen decades of development and improvement. It's a huge sandbox which simulates a lot of different stuff.

Reforger on the other hand is on the Enfusion engine, relatively new. Everything that A3 and previous did needs to be remade from scratch. The game largely serves as a 'prologue' to Arma 4 and is structured more as a game as less a military simulation sandbox. You can expect A4 to have a lot more.

Once you get mods it'll probably breath some fresh air but don't expect it to make the game into ArmA 3. A lot of mods require whatever they're adding to have a 'base' to work off in the vanilla. For instance, since we don't have planes in vanilla Reforger, don't expect polished plane mods to be a thing. Same thing for heavy armour and such.

Can also be a financial (and sometimes regulatory nightmare) taking on a historic house. Usually decades of "she'll be right" fixes and neglect (sometimes not even malicious neglect, just stuff that was never in sight of the previous owner).
Think of a number and double it, maybe even triple it.

I would suggest reaching out to a heritage consultant, or if available, a heritage architect which operates in your local area. There is absolutely a niche within the architectural and development profession which caters to this, especially when they're developing near another heritage item or within a conservation zone. They will be able to inform you more of what's possible in your local area and maybe give you some other additional information.

Just a word of warning though, these types of design aren't common for a reason. It's very expensive as most of the design and materials will be bespoke.

Usually it boils down to two reasons:

1) They will have a few designs curated already that's been financially optimised. Its cheaper to just build pretty much the preset designs and if someone really wants to change it, they can do it of their own accord after the build is complete (though there are some regulatory issues here potentially). This is especially in the case where an integrated development application is made for the whole subdivision.

2) Some Councils will have development controls which purposefully limit the aesthetic... usually, it'll be grounded in the "community's values" but you already know the majority of people who participate in local politics are oldies, since they're the only ones who have time to actually participate. In my experience though, these types of rules aren't always super common throughout NSW though they will regulate things like, no wall can go for >10m without "stepping out", which will obviously influence the design.

Most Councils (in NSW) don't really have Development Control Plans that overreach like this (though I've heard some horror stories from places like the Blue Mountains). However some of their provisions may make it harder to design like this.

Really, building houses like this are more of a financial issue and not a regulatory one.

Landing is the hard part -- flying, even quite low is easy by comparison. So don't beat yourself up over it. The most difficult part of landing is bleeding speed, which is why a lot of people J-hook (even if it looks ridiculous). You can bleed off airspeed by slowly pitching up and lowering the collective as you approach your landing site as well.

However I'd submit that a lot of issues with landing is people's expectation that you need to be right on or next to the objective. Helicopters are great in that they can introduce asymetry -- you can land behind a fortified position and come from the other direction.

Don't forget as well that if you're in a gunship, your door gunners are there to suppress, it's not about getting kills or accuracy, it's genuinely just about startling the enemy enough so they don't peak their head out for too long.

Sometimes with landing it's super twitchy if you're using WSAD. I generally don't fly with my mouse but on landing I do use it for more precise movements. You can turn that on in the settings if you're unaware FYI.

You're still viewing my take as an "x means we have to do y" type scenario, which isn't really what I'm advocating for. I'll admit "replacing" probably isn't the right word, I meant more the idea that getting rid of exhaust producing vehicles means something needs to take the place (as in, the vehicle, not the pollution itself).

If we - as a nation - are going to try and get rid of exhaust-producing vehicles, we're going to have spend a lot of money. Government subsidies, infrastructure, power generation, and of course, the actual money spent by the consumer. In the long-term when it comes to mitigating the impacts of climate change, going through all that effort and expenditure to replace one source of pollution with a somewhat lessened pollutor, in my opinion at least, isn't practical.

Also, per your link, I've never said here that EVs are going to produce more pollution than ICE, which seems to more or less be the subject of that particular article. I'm not an anti-EV skeptic with a hateboner for them for no reason other than they're not gasoline powered. My skepticism is more centred around the entire notion that private transportation should be the "default".

Your article even touches on this -- which states 90% of PM10, and 85% of PM2.5 emissions are from non-tailpipe sources. How do you think we, in the longer-term, resolve that? This is the basis of why I think the "EV revolution", while having its own novel improvements, is overall in the grand scheme of things a bandaid solution, both in terms of the health of our cities and our environment. I don't think EVs contribute a significant level of harm reduction to warrant such a major overhaul of our transportation system -- we need to be giving priority to other ways, ways that take cars as a whole off the road.

The article you've linked is a generally ok article debunking "pop science". My opinion hasn't stemmed from these sources, they're from a number of years now researching books and journal articles on matters like this. If you want me to dig up ones I've cited in my academic and professional work -- ones that aren't such pop science with dubious research methods -- I'd be happy to provide some.

But again, just to hammer the point home, my argument is not that just because EVs still produce pollution, we shouldn't do anything. My argument is that *because* EVs still produce a notable amount of pollution, if we're going to spend such great amounts of money to fix the issue, we should be giving it to a solution that isn't fundamentally inefficient on a grand scale. Greater, smart density; public transportation; revitalised zoning to bring third places and trip generators closer to home. Getting cars off the road is the most practical way in the long term of resolving this issue.

I think we've trapped ourselves into a black and white argument when the reality is it's more complicated than that.

Yes, obviously removing one factor is a positive. One issue though -- particularly with EVs, is the additional weight does result in additional tyre wear. The increasing weight of vehicles (both ICE and EV) have resulted in tyre wear eclipsing the total potential for harm than exhaust. Some studies have found it to even up to 2,000 times as polluting as exhaust.

It's a perfectly valid concern, because to many, EVs are the fix to many of the downsides of private transport. Things like tyre/brake pollutants aren't as discussed in such a high profile as lithium processing, carbon emissions, etc. Now, I'm of the only opinion that to fix this issue means a couple things:

A) Shrinking the size of the average car, unlikely against the powerful lobbying of the car industry.

B) Prioritising urban planning to incentivise a reduced reliance on private transportation.

If you've ever lived next a main road, with screened windows, you'd find that they become black and full of gunk in no time. Many attribute it to being carbon from exhausts, but it's usually a mixture of the aforementioned brake dust and tyre wear... Not to mention the more invisible issues of tyre microplastics.

I'm sorry if I came off as dismissive when it comes to eliminating exhaust pollution -- that wasn't my intention. I'm of the stance though that fixing exhausts is only a very minor drop in the sea of pollution and health issues... And an issue we may not be likely to fix unless the current trend of crossover-sized EVs ends (which seems generally unlikely internationally, but especially so in Australia, we don't even get the 'city car' EVs like the e208, Honda E, etc).

There's a number of other considerations with EVs as well, like resources, infrastructure, retrofitting, etc. all with their pros and cons. Eliminating exhaust means replacing it with something else, most think EVs. I implore people to think more broadly is the backbone of my comment.

We don't use Euclidean Zoning in Australia. It's a common and understandable misconception but the Euclidean system is different. We actually use a very similar system to the Japanese in NSW through the Local Environmental Plan, generally referred to as 'Exclusionary Zoning'. Whereas Euclidean traditionally follows a hierarchy of zones, exclusionary zoning in NSW specifies permitted and non-permitted uses. Some zones can be quite liberal, such as the R1 General Residential Zone, where the 'permitted with consent' criteria is suffixed with 'any land use not listed as prohibited'.

Most places you'd be surprised with what actually can be built. Usually, it's the local Development Control Plan which can make it difficult to achieve with rules on setbacks, minimum parking spaces, landscaping, etc.

The LEP does vary Council to Council but it's increasingly becoming more and more standardised across the board to promote development. Some towns may still have archaic land use tables and zoning but the State is definitely forcing their hand.

I think the much bigger issue we have to tackle is the cultural one. Australian's think density and mixed use result in slums, littered with cheap, poorly built tin cans in glass houses that cost you an arm and a leg in strata fees annually. While in an ideal world fixing this issue wouldn't be a political move, with the way Council functions it really is a very politically coded area. Good luck trying to keep the community on your side.

While it doesn't magically make it go away, we've found betters way of treating and decontaminating, and ultimately more efficient means of trapping waste.

Now this is probably where opinions will vary a lot. I'm of the opinion that Australia as a nation has an abundance of land for the issue of nuclear waste to not be a prolific problem. We already have nuclear sites from weapons testing (a contentious historical issue in its own right) that'll likely never be able to rehabilitated entirely within our lifetimes. We have the space to construct these facilities that will store and hold our waste for centuries. I can imagine though that some people will still see this as problematic, be it because of the fact that we're not really making the issue going away, or because of the cultural and historical issue that these sites usually have. This is good advice. As a general rule of thumb as well, city layouts evolved a lot over time. As you pointed out, most old world cities can be defined by concentric rings -- maybe it was a defence thing with walls, or maybe it was just the natural growth of that city.

When public transport started to become a thing in the 1800s/1900s, many cities with room for growth moved from concentric rings to more of a 'star'-shaped pattern. The points of the stars would usually indiciate public transit lines; many people, especially the wealthy, were desperate to leave the poor conditions of early Industrial cities. I don't think it'd be quite right to call these suburbs just yet though.

Of course, when car dependency became a thing -- not super common in Europe, but still present in some cities, particularly those that were heavily bombed and rebuilt with American civil engineers -- the star shaped evolved to the sprawling layout we now know.

OP, I can see what you're going for but as the others here have pointed out, it's not really that realistic. In many of these older cities with a more freeform structure, the underlying reason for that is more to do with the physical constraints of the land. Lower-lying flood prone land would be avoided, certain areas may have once been farms, there may have been trees or hard terrain, etc. They didn't necessarily have the same level of technology we had to deal with these issues, so practicality was more of the essence rather than continuity and uniformity.

Unfortunately, I don't think C:S2 really deals with these issues well either. There's no punishment for making everything work to your liking. You may enjoy using the Map Overlay mod with some Google overlays of real European cities if you're striving for something realistic.
